text: If you had a free afternoon to explore something new, which pulls you in most?

options.text: Tinkering with a gadget, app, or piece of tech to see how it works.
Reading about a scientific discovery or watching a documentary on how the universe works.
Sketching, designing, or making something visually creative.
Going for a walk outdoors, noticing plants, animals, or weather.

text: A friend asks for advice about a problem they're having with their group project. What do you naturally do?

options.text: Listen closely and help them think through the group dynamics.
Ask for the details of exactly what happened so you understand the situation precisely.
Think about how to reorganize the group to run more efficiently.

text: Pick the task you'd rather spend a free Saturday on.

options.text: Building or fixing something physical (furniture, a bike, a small circuit).
Writing a story, composing music, or making art for its own sake.
Neither really appeals to me.

text: Which puzzle would you rather spend twenty minutes on?

options.text: A logic or number puzzle with one correct, elegant solution.
A case study about why a small shop's sales are dropping.

text: In a group project at school or college, which role do you gravitate toward?

options.text: The one who researches and organizes the information / structures the report.
The one who builds or codes the actual thing.
The one who designs how it looks or is presented.

text: A recipe serves 4 and needs 250g of rice. You need to serve 11 people. How do you figure out how much rice to use?

options.text: Set up a ratio and calculate it precisely (250/4 x 11).
Estimate roughly - 'a bit less than triple' and round generously.
I'd look it up or ask someone rather than calculate it myself.

text: Which of these is the odd one out, and why: lecture, tutorial, mentorship, textbook?

options.text: 'Textbook' - the others involve a live person guiding you, this one doesn't.
'Mentorship' - it's more personal and long-term than the others.
Not sure - I'd need more time to think about it than this allows.

text: Picture folding a flat square piece of paper in half twice, then cutting a small triangle off one folded corner. When unfolded, how many holes will there be? How did you get your answer?

options.text: I mentally pictured the folds and unfolds and counted the holes.
I guessed a plausible-sounding number.
I'd need to actually fold paper to know for sure.

text: Your team's weekly meeting keeps running over time and nothing gets decided. What's your first move?

options.text: List out exactly why it's happening, step by step, before proposing a fix.
Suggest a completely different format for the meeting altogether.
Let it keep happening; it's not really my problem to fix.

text: Sequence: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ... What's the next number, and how did you find it?

options.text: Noticed the gaps increase by 2 each time (4,6,8,10) and continued the pattern to get 42.
Recognized it as n(n+1) and computed the next value directly.
Couldn't work it out, so I guessed.

text: Which work setup sounds better to you?

options.text: I get a goal and figure out my own way to reach it.
I get a clear, step-by-step process to follow.

text: You're assigned a big task. Which do you prefer?

options.text: Working with a small team, bouncing ideas back and forth throughout.
Owning it myself and checking in only at milestones.
Working alongside others but mostly on my own sub-part.

text: Your manager or teacher gives you a task with almost no instructions and says 'figure out what's needed.' How do you feel?

options.text: Energized - I like defining the problem myself.
Uncomfortable - I'd rather ask a lot of clarifying questions first.
Anxious, but I'd push through anyway.

text: Which week would you enjoy more?

options.text: Deep, focused work on one thing for the whole week.
Several different tasks or projects, switching between them daily.
A fast-moving week with tight deadlines and constant momentum.

text: Picture your ideal workday. Which is closer?

options.text: A clear schedule, regular check-ins, defined responsibilities.
Long stretches of unstructured time with lots of interaction with others throughout.
Long stretches of quiet, independent focus time.

text: Imagine two job offers, otherwise similar. Which would you choose?

options.text: Higher pay and more financially rewarding, but less job security.
Lower pay but very stable and secure.
Lower pay but constantly intellectually challenging and stimulating.

text: What would make you feel most proud of a piece of work?

options.text: Knowing I achieved something genuinely difficult, regardless of who notices.
Being recognized publicly and respected for it.
Knowing it actually helped or changed something for other people.

text: Which future bothers you least?

options.text: A demanding career that leaves little personal time, but I control my own decisions at work.
A flexible, low-stress career that leaves plenty of time for personal life.
A career where I can live and work from anywhere, on my own terms.

text: Rank what matters most to you in a future job: being well paid, feeling secure, or doing meaningful/impactful work. Which comes first?

options.text: Being well paid comes first for me.
Feeling secure comes first for me.
Doing meaningful, impactful work comes first for me.

text: Your first job: which manager would you rather have?

options.text: One who checks in often, explains what's expected and backs you up when things go wrong.
One who gives you a goal and leaves you alone until you need them.
Honestly, I'd rather not have a manager at all.

text: You made a mistake that cost your team a deadline. What would help you most the next day?

options.text: A senior sitting down with me to go over what happened, without blame.
Being left to fix it myself so I can prove I can.
Knowing the team still has my back.

text: How much does it matter to you that your organisation treats people fairly, even if the pay is a bit lower?

options.text: Hardly at all, pay comes first.
A little.
Quite a lot.
It's a dealbreaker for me.

text: A classmate is struggling with a topic you understand well. The exam is in two days and you're also behind. What do you do?

options.text: Spend an evening explaining it to them. I actually enjoy that.
Send them good notes or a video, then focus on my own prep.
Focus on myself first. I'll help after the exam.

text: Which of these would feel most rewarding at the end of a day?

options.text: Someone told me I really helped them.
I finally understood something that had confused me for weeks.
I made something that looks or sounds exactly how I imagined it.
I convinced a group to go with my plan and it worked.

text: Rank what you'd want people to say about your work in five years. Pick the one that matters most.

options.text: "They're one of the best in their field."
"They quietly do excellent work."
"They made a real difference to people."
"They built something of their own."

text: Two internship offers, same pay. One is at a well-known company where you'd do routine tasks. The other is at an unknown startup where you'd own a real project. Which do you take?

options.text: The well-known name. It opens doors.
The startup. I'd rather do work that matters.
Whichever has the better mentor.

text: Quick task: list as many uses as you can for an old cycle tyre in 30 seconds. How many did you get?

options.text: 0 to 2
3 to 5
6 to 8
9 or more

text: Your college fest needs a theme and nobody has an idea. What's your move?

options.text: Throw out a bunch of wild ideas until one sticks.
Look at what worked in past years and improve on it.
Get everyone in a room and lead the brainstorm.

text: Which kind of week sounds better to you?

options.text: Lots happening at once, quick decisions, a bit chaotic.
A steady rhythm where I can go deep on one thing.
Different tasks each day, but nothing rushed.

text: When an exam is only two days away, how do you usually work?

options.text: I actually focus best under that pressure.
I'd have planned so I'm not rushing.
I get stressed and my work suffers.

text: Your phone suddenly stops connecting to Wi-Fi, though everyone else's works. What do you do first?

options.text: Work through it step by step: restart, forget the network, check settings.
Search online for exactly why this happens.
Hand it to someone who's good with phones.

text: Puzzle: A shop sells pens at 3 for 20 rupees. How much do 12 pens cost? (Pick what you'd answer without a calculator.)

options.text: 80 rupees
60 rupees
I'd need to work it out on paper.

text: Which school or college subject felt most like you, regardless of marks?

options.text: Physics, chemistry or biology
Accounts, economics or business studies
Psychology, sociology or languages
Art, music or design

text: Organising your group's trip: which part would you volunteer for?

options.text: The budget spreadsheet and who-paid-what.
Negotiating the hotel price and bookings.
Making sure everyone's included and happy.
Planning the route and driving.

text: How do you feel about doing the same kind of task every day if you're good at it?

options.text: I'd love that, it's comfortable.
Fine for a while.
I'd get restless after a few months.
I'd get bored within weeks.

text: Would you rather start your own thing with uncertain income, or have a stable salary doing interesting work?

options.text: Start my own thing.
Stable salary, interesting work.
Stable job first, my own thing later.

text: In a group project, which role do you naturally end up in?

options.text: I take a clear piece and do it on my own.
I coordinate and keep everyone on track.
I work closely with one or two people on the hardest bit.
I end up redoing other people's parts so it's right.
